evals.prompt: How much text and compute went into training large language models, by the course's illustrations?
evals.expected_output: Reading GPT-3's training text non-stop would take a human over 2,600 years; at one billion operations per second, training the largest models would take well over 100 million years.
expectations: States over 2,600 years of non-stop reading for GPT-3's text (lesson 05 ~99s)

evals.prompt: Why use mini-batches instead of the full gradient, and what does it cost?
evals.expected_output: Summing the influence of every training example per step is too slow; shuffle and split into mini-batches (e.g. 100 examples), step on each: not the exact gradient (a 'drunk man stumbling downhill') but a good approximation and a big speedup. This is stochastic gradient descent.
expectations: Says computing over all examples per step is too slow and mini-batches give a significant speedup (lesson 03 ~573-605s)
Says the step is only an approximation of the true gradient / stochastic gradient descent (lesson 03 ~605-635s)

evals.prompt: What does raising or lowering the temperature do when sampling from GPT-3, and is there a cap?
evals.expected_output: Temperature T divides the exponents in softmax: larger T flattens the distribution (less likely words, more original but can degenerate into nonsense); T=0 always picks the most likely word (a trite Goldilocks story). The API does not allow T above 2, an arbitrary constraint.
expectations: Says higher T makes the distribution more uniform and T=0 always picks the most predictable word (lesson 06 ~1435-1466s)
Says the API caps temperature at 2 (lesson 06 ~1498s)

evals.prompt: Where do GPT-3's 175 billion parameters live: how much in attention vs the MLP blocks?
evals.expected_output: Attention: ~58B (about a third); MLPs: up and down projections ~604M each, ~1.2B per block, x96 = ~116B (about two thirds); the rest is embedding/unembedding.
expectations: States ~58B in attention, about a third (lesson 07 ~1461s)
States ~116B in MLPs, about two thirds (lesson 08 ~963-994s)

evals.prompt: Where in the course is superposition introduced, and what is the idea?
evals.expected_output: Lesson 08 (How might LLMs store facts) around 17:37 (1057 s): individual neurons rarely represent one clean feature; in high dimensions many nearly perpendicular directions fit (exponentially many), so a model can store far more features than dimensions.
expectations: Points to lesson 08 at a timestamp within 60 s of 1057 s
